utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before Mr. Moore starts, may I remind you, Mr. Sljivancanin, of the affirmation which you made which still applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, before we commence this morning, as I say, we have four files to put before the witness and the Court. I'd like to deal, if I may, with the first file of documents and have those handed out now, if I may, please. The title will be "Military documents and miscellaneous." The interpreters have got their documents already. May I just explain how the document operates. I hope and trust that there is an index at the front which should be two pages indicating that there are 32 tabs referring to exhibits. If we take, by way of example, tab 1 is in the English, tab 2 is the B/C/S version. That system follows the whole way through with two exceptions. That was the problem we had yesterday. Tab 17 and tab 18, they will have the B/C/S immediately behind. So when one goes to 17, you'll find an excerpt from a paper and there is the B/C/S version itself. The other files are fairly similar in structure. Can I assist Your Honour in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's beyond your capacity from there, Mr. Moore, but I will plod along trying to find the transcript on the screen soon. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, that's very kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, when I refer to documents, I will try to refer to the tab numbers on the right-hand side. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes - good morning, Mr. Moore - I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sljivancanin. Can we deal, please, can tab 3 and tab 4. Tab 3 is the English version; tab 4 is the B/C/S version. It is known as Exhibit 396. Do you have your regulations, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, regulations on the application of international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to deal, if I may, as we can see, there is a large series of contents but I would like to deal with the various rules, and just dealing with it in fairly brief order, if we look at rule 20, we can see that it refers specifically to "Personal responsibility for violations of the laws of war." I just read it so it goes into the record: "Every individual, a member of the military or a civilian, shall be personally accountable for violations of the laws of war if he or she commits a violation himself, herself, or orders one to be committed. Ignorance of the provisions of the laws of war does not exonerate the transgressors from responsibility." Would it be fair to say that you were aware in what I will call general terms, perhaps even specific terms, of this provision, what is called a basic provision?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time at the military academy, I studied regulations and the laws. We also studied international laws of war and, yes, I was familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. There are basically four paragraphs in this article. The third clearly relates to liability before an international court. And then thirdly -- I should say fourthly: "A person organising, inciting, or assisting in the commission in a violation of the laws of war, or an accomplice in the same, shall also be held responsible as a perpetrator." Can I take it that in relation to your last answer, you were also aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move to Article 21 which, to some extent, is inaccurately titled. Let us proceed with that. It says: "Responsibility for the actions of subordinates." That's in highlights, but the content is different, I would suggest. "An officer shall be personally liable for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that units subordinate to him," note the next word, "or other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violations and at a time when it was still possible to prevent their commission failed to take measures to prevent such violations. That officer shall also be held personally liable who, aware that violations of the laws of war have been committed, fails to institute disciplinary or criminal proceedings against the offender, or if the instituting of proceedings does not fall within his jurisdiction, fails to report the violation to his superior officer." The title says "Responsibility for the action of subordinates," but I would suggest to you that this particular section is much wider. It relates to subordinate units or other units or individuals. Now, you attended various courses and colleges, you reached a high rank within the JNA. Would it be right to say that you were aware of the responsibility that this particular article created?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an officer, I was always fully aware of the fact that the responsibility was mine; also for training my subordinates and that I was to answer for any of their actions in my area. I didn't go that thoroughly through each and every item of these regulations, but I'm familiar with the international provisions. And based on what you've just read out, my subordinates were security officers in my own unit. I did not have any units that were subordinated to me. I didn't know or indeed notice at the time that any crimes were committed. As for this unit that I was responsible for as chief of security, and you must be aware of that based on my reports, all those individuals who committed minor disciplinary infractions were sent away from the unit and steps were taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we please come back to the question, and that is, it says clearly in relation to the action of subordinates but there were two other categories, one is other units, clearly referring to units that were not subordinated to him, or individuals, who actually relate to civilians, and is a logical follow-up of Article 20. So it's not just units subordinated; it is units general and civilian. You were aware of that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that you are a much better lawyer than I am, and I am also certain that your interpretation of these laws and provisions must be convenient for you as a lawyer. As I said, I am familiar with these regulations and laws. I did study these at the military academy. Everything that I did, I did in the spirit of the laws and regulations that applied. I also know that all of my subordinates were working in keeping with all the laws and regulations that applied at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Look, let's set aside all the lawyer/officer elements. What this actual says is just common sense. It says as an officer, if a unit is subordinated to you, you should try and stop it or deal with it. As an officer, if you know other units are going to be involved, you become -- you either stop it or deal with it. And if it's a civilian that is going on, you deal with it the same way. It is just a question of common sense. It's not fancy lawyer's construction, is it? It's just common sense; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course both as an officer, and as a human being, it is my duty to fight any crime or any criminal action. However, within my area of responsibility alone, and within my area of influence, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's look at the core section or the core of Article 21. It says, in relation to planning the commission of such violations: "... and at a time when it was still possible to prevent their commission." What that means, I'd suggest, is if a criminal act has commenced, and there is the responsibility of stopping that criminal act continuing, Article 21 puts a duty upon such an officer to intervene. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer is duty-bound to intervene right away, as soon as he gets wind of any sort of suspicion at all. However, where I was at the time, I had not heard of any crimes being committed or indeed planned. As I said, even when we had completely minor disciplinary infractions by certain soldiers or territorials and volunteers, if you like, we foiled those and nipped them in the bud. We would send these people to the military remand prison in Belgrade - there's a letter about that, about the forensics from the military police patrol - and such soldiers would immediately be sent away from our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is the significance of the final passage in that article, namely: "... fails to report the violation to his superior officer"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance is important. It means that every officer must report even minor disciplinary infractions and not only crimes. He must request measures to be taken in cases where he is unable to take any steps himself. At the time, I never, at any point in time, had anything at all to indicate that anyone had committed any crimes of the magnitude under consideration here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does this article apply to Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain yesterday, Mr. Moore. I took the stand as a human being, as an officer, as a witness. I told you what my reasons were. My intention was to tell you everything I know. It is not as a judge or as a lawyer that I am now sitting here. I can't interpret these for you and tell you who this might or might not be in relation to. This applies to all JNA officers equally since the rules apply to the JNA as a whole. It's difficult to name names and to individualise. I think this applies to all officers equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if that is your answer, that will suffice. Let us -- I will come back to this section in all probability in due course, but let us know, please, move to tab 1 for the English and tab 2 for the B/C/S. For the record, this relates to Exhibit 107. It's called "The rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And I want to deal, if I may, please, with something that Mr. Lukic had dealt with but rather briefly. It relates to, in English, page 7, starting "the tasks of security organs," and it is number 6. Would you have that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I said to you yesterday: Did you accept whether the security organ was -- I will amend it slightly, an additional set of eyes and ears for the commander and the command? Let us look, then, at what the task of the security organ actually are as specified. "6: Security organs are responsible for the detection, tracking, and prevention of intelligence activities and other activities of foreign military intelligence," it seems to be non-military intelligence, "... and the activities of hostile Yugoslav immigration carried out in the country or from abroad or aimed against the armed forces and the preparation of the armed forces for the country's defence while JNA security organs also deal with activities aimed against organisations for NVO." So whether it applies in the Vukovar scenario, here there is reflection to -- or reference to detection, tracking, and prevention. You obviously accept that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, again, I must say that I do not accept that at all. I, as a security organ, was there in a technical capacity and had technical tasks. What it says right here, "detection, tracking and prevention" and that's quite specific, "of foreign military intelligence services." Now that makes more than just a blight bit of difference, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to indicate, Mr. Sljivancanin, is what the function is of the security organ. I am accepting that this may not apply to Vukovar, but I'm referring to the function of the security organ, and it is detection, tracking, and prevention. Look at B, if you may, please. "The detection and prevention of hostile activities by individuals, groups or organisations, against the armed forces and members of the armed forces while JNA security organs also deal with activities against organisations for NVO and persons employed in these organisations," and goes on. But again, "detection, prevention, of hostile activities by individuals, groups, and organisations." Doesn't that suggest a proactive role, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While answering Mr. Lukic's questions and while answering yours, I said what you're reading from are tasks of which security organs are the focal points, and it is quite true that under B, it says what you just quoted, "hostile activities by individuals, groups or organisations against the armed forces and members of the armed forces." If you, Mr. Moore, or the Court have enough time, I can give you an example of some work that I did precisely along these lines and that will illustrate my understanding of this particular issue. If there is no time available, then I would say that what you have just read out is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Sljivancanin. You have three counsel, and they are able to deal with any points who have been dealing with this matter at some length, I think, for almost four days. So I'm asking you a simple question: B refers to the Vukovar scenario, doesn't it? It refers to social order established by the constitution of the SFRY, threatening the country's security, threatening the armed forces or breaching the secrecy of the plans and preparation of the armed forces for the country's defence. You went into Vukovar as the JNA, still believing in Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there as a JNA member. We had received an assignment from our Superior Command. I believed in that country. I believed that it would survive. I tried to deal with all my tasks in a regular and proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When the phrase "detection and prevention of hostile activities by individuals, groups, and organisations," basically against the constitution of the SFRY, it would be right to say that the persons who were in Croatia, in Vukovar, what I will call, for convenience, the Croatian defenders of Vukovar, fall within that category, don't they? They were fighting against Yugoslavia. They were trying to achieve the dissolution of the constitution of Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you're asking me, I don't agree with the term "Vukovar's defenders." We were all defenders. It really very much depends on your point of view, doesn't it? What I call them, what I choose to call them, is Croat paramilitary units. As far as that's concerned, I personally at the time believed that the Croatian people were not against Yugoslavia and that for me as a security organ, the paramount thing was to track down and bring in the leaders of this armed insurrection, those who were behind the whole thing, or even possibly as we relate at all by those we captured had mobilised certain people by force and given them weapons to man the barricades. For me, it was the instigators of that whole thing that were to blame. If those 10 or 15 men could have been brought to justice at the time, maybe the whole situation would have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But 6(B) specifically deals with the situation in Vukovar, doesn't it? As you perceived it.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rule does not specifically refer to Vukovar but to general tasks, and I have explained how I perceive a general task. These are tasks specified against anyone subverting the constitutional order and eroding the system which functioned in Yugoslavia at the time. All those who armed themselves irregularly, illegally, and opened fire at members of the Yugoslav People's Army, which at that time was a regular army, were perpetrators of criminally fences. And I as the security organ then thought - and I repeat - I never believe the Croatian people to be against Yugoslavia but individuals who incited and indeed forced people to bear arms were against Yugoslavia, and that those people, those individuals were to be brought to justice and that everything should have been done in order to prevent them from pursuing their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just taking that answer, do you accept that persons who wilfully opened fire at members of the Yugoslav People's Army, which, as you say, was a regular army at the time, that they were "... subverting the constitutional order and eroding the system which functioned as Yugoslavia at that time"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them were eroding the system. They were committing criminal offences which can be punished according to specific articles of the law, or some persons may have been mislead. But I consider then and I consider today that the system was eroded by individuals who organised themselves for reasons known to them, and they also incited other people to transgress in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And that would be eroding or subverting the constitutional order, isn't that right, as you perceived it at that time. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Any armed insurgency is tantamount to an erosion of the constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to C. I'll deal with these matters, I hope, a bit quicker. C relates to the implementation of measures and operations of counter-intelligence and relates to territories, zones in respect of the country's defence. So implementation is a very active involvement for the security organ, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item C presupposes the implementation of measures and operations of counter-intelligence tasks which are extremely important in the work of security organs. And these counter-intelligence tasks primarily involve the protection of plans, of facilities, of documents, of persons of significance to the armed forces, and generally what was of relevance and of importance to the armed forces for the defence of the country. And that is counter-intelligence work. Counter-intelligence work is one of the difficult and labourious tasks pursued and carried out by organs of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: D, the gathering and verification of information for the operational needs of security organs and the running of security checks on persons for recruitment into the armed forces. So that is the security organ checking that whoever comes into the army is a person who can be trusted. It doesn't perhaps apply so much in Vukovar, but that is one of the tasks, isn't it? It's very proactive.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, sir, one of my very important tasks as the security organ was that we had to check out all people assuming duty in the Guards Brigade, including soldiers. I have talked about the structure, the composition of the soldiers sent to us in 1991 from doing their military service because they were deliberately planted on us, some territorial organs from all other Yugoslavia who were better aware of the ideas about the disintegration of Yugoslavia than I was. That is why this verification of staff was important for us because you had to give a rifle, ammunition, weapons to this young person and to assign him to a certain -- to secure a certain person, and if that young person was a psychopath and unstable and wields a rifle, he could create lots of problems. Because the Guards Brigade troops were, in contrast to others, always -- always carried live ammunition for the discharge of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal with F, please. I'd like you to read this specifically with Vukovar in mind. "The organisation and maintenance of the security organ's information system for the purpose of analysing data and intelligence, reporting, informing, controlling, and guiding within the competence of the security organ and in accordance with these rules or regulations and general enactments." Now, how can you possibly say that the security organ is not the eyes and ears of a command with 6(F) being actively pursued?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see this item differently. We, as the security organs in our department, were to undertake an analysis of our work and to undertake annual analysis of the tasks, including the collection of data and other things in order to gain some experience, and to do that, we had to develop information systems. At some later point that involved the introduction of computers. We had -- this item actually more deals with the annual analysis of the work of the security organs. This is the way I see item F, and this is the way we see item F.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, analysing data and intelligence can also relate for information coming in from the SSNO, can't it? Reports coming in about who's actively involved? Doesn't it also apply to your secret network that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An analysis is undertaken of all data, of all information coming in. We had some short-term analyses, monthly ones, but the most important analyses and the information processing was on an annual basis, when he summed up the experiences and proposed new measures to improve the methods of work and to check whether we had been properly using the methods of security organs. Of course I was only there for two years. I'm not a great expert on security, so that that is as much as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect to you, Mr. Sljivancanin, two years is an extremely long time and that does not exonerate you in any way from the responsibilities that you had in Vukovar, so let's make it absolutely clear. "Intelligence," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Intelligence" means gathering data on such persons and all those who have been infiltrated to work against the unit in which I am the security organ, or to pursue any intelligence work on their part in order to gain insight into the situation, the combat readiness of it, or to influence the men of the unit to erode through them the combat readiness of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I, in simplistic terms put "intelligence" in the following way: Intelligence would imply intelligence from within the army, within the units at that time, and intelligence externally coming in from other units or organisations like the SSNO. That's one limb of the intelligence operation you would operate on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, in the Yugoslav People's Army, there is a security organ, and then there is an intelligence organ. Well, to put it in the simplest of terms and briefest of terms, the security organ namely -- fought against the intelligence organs against others who targeted the JNA in their activities. And the intelligence organ of the JNA collected the data that you are referring to from others. Meaning I pursued a counter-intelligence activity and these others pursued an intelligence activity. That would be it in briefest terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that is not correct. I would suggest to you that you were gaining intelligence from individual soldiers, as you suggested to us, when you were talking to them in the front line, finding out about their combat readiness, finding about their morale, finding out exactly if there were any problems. Do you accept that or not as a general concept?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that in Vukovar, I was on the front line. I consider that to have been an armed rebellion, and I was collecting intelligence, collecting data in my own country, on my own territory, who were the spear-heads of the armed rebellion, what weapons they had, and whether I could reach them and bring them to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask the question again: Do you accept, as a general principle, that you were gathering intelligence from your soldiers, JNA soldiers, about their morale, about their combat readiness, about their fatigue, about any other problems that were existing at that time? Do you accept that or not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it intelligence. I would say that these were regular bits of information that I was interested in in terms of what the situation in the unit in which I was chief of security was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will use the word "information." So you accept that as the first head. Secondly, do you accept that you were receiving information from other organisations, for example, the SSNO, giving you information about what may be happening in Vukovar or other areas? Do you accept that as a second head?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said here, I've shown that from the chief of security of the cabinet of the federal secretary I received information which he received from the security administration, referring to the organisers of the armed rebellion in Vukovar at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I will suggest to you that the answer to that is "yes." Thirdly, do you accept that you were attempting to obtain information about who was actually fighting against you, the actual persons and numbers. You knew about Jastreb but other names. You were looking for other names as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's no secret we were looking for persons who were the organisers and -- of the armed rebellion and the ringleaders of everything that had happened in Vukovar. Inter alia, I looked the most for Jastreb. I knew, having received information from the competent organs, that he was a former colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, and I believe that he was from the aerial observation and alert service and reporting service. And I wanted to meet with him so that we could talk as human beings. And I drew attention to the fact that it was ugly that our common soldiers would -- should be killing each other. And I wanted to talk about these things with him as a human being and to let the people decide rather than fight, because we had coexisted happily together until recently. Why we should be fighting? That was the idea that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, if you could just try and focus on the questions. I am saying you were trying to find out who you were fighting against, names, and also numbers, units. That is correct, isn't it? I'd suggest it's perfectly obvious.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm telling you what I was thinking about at the time. I cannot give you answers which you will find suitable. My initial desire was to meet with Mr. Jastreb, and I believe that if we met, that as two officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, we would be able to find a solution in order not to fight each other and kill each other. I was convinced of that. Now, what kind of an answer you would like me to give you, I don't know. I'm giving you my own feelings, what my wishes were. Believe me, as a man, please don't try to extract the answer from me which you would like me to give you. I'm really telling you what was in my heart and in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the fourth category, and I'm not saying that they are absolute, but for convenience in cross-examination, you were trying to ascertain whom you saw was responsible for this rebellion, the 10 or 14 people; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the fighting progressed, and as more and more people got killed, and when Mr. Vance told me that the Croatian people regarded the Yugoslav People's Army as an aggressor, well, frankly, it occurred to me why use force? Why do this? Let us save what we can and do everything that we can in order to save the captured men and officers of the Yugoslav People's Army and let the politicians deal with this matter. So later I said that as many members of the paramilitary units should be taken in, brought in, in order to be exchanged for our own soldiers and officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you use the word "kravatski" here in court 15 years on, but you didn't use the word "kravatski" in your reports, did you? You used the word "Ustasha"; isn't that correct? Or are you saying you've never used the word "Ustasha" in any formal document?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the word "Ustashas" because the very people with whom I was communicating via the radio station called themselves Ustashas and they were proud of it. Actually, I found that word alien, and from studying the history of the peoples of Yugoslavia - because I knew that in the Second World War the Ustashas had aligned themselves with the fascists - if that history was interpreted to me accurately, that is what we learned. And I thought, I never considered the entire Croatian people Ustasha but those who opened fire at the innocent members of the Yugoslav People's Army and the innocent civilians and called themselves Ustashas to boot, I considered them Ustashas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the word "Ustasha" to a Serb had a very specific meaning, didn't it? Ustasha had originally allied themselves with the Nazis and had fought against the partisans. That is correct, isn't it? And it is a pejorative word for a Serb to use against a Croat; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, let me tell you, I told you what I had studied and learned from books in school as a young person. The Ustashas in the territory of Yugoslavia, just like the Chetniks for that matter, were considered to be traitors in the Second World War, aligned with the fascists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's look on, please, at the security organs participate in [sic], because I'm suggesting, as I said to you yesterday, you were eyes and ears. Number 7: "Security organs participate in the detection and prevention of serious crimes that involve the theft of or damage to arms, ammunition, combat, equipment, mines and explosive devices and other types of serious property crime in the armed forces," and then relates to other matters. Can we work on the basis that attacking, beating, and abusing individuals who are in the trust of the JNA would fall within this category? Can we work on that basis?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tasks which we enumerated before are the basic tasks for which the security organs are responsible principally, but in these that you enumerated now are tasks that they participate in but they are not the principal protagonists of. And this is one of the tasks that they should be participating in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what this actually says, again, common sense, is that you participate in the detection and prevention of serious crimes, and serious crimes clearly would include beating of prisoner of war or individuals who had been taken prisoner by the JNA forces. That's right, isn't it? It falls quite clearly within your ambit?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not written -- the word "beating of prisoners of war" is not referred to in this item. It just refers to damage to arms, serious property crime in the armed forces, threatening defence capability, combat readiness. This is what the item refers to. I don't see beating referred to anywhere in this item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's my fault. What I am trying to suggest is that here you are involved in the prevention and detection of serious crimes. They refer to theft and damage to arms, but it refers clearly to the prevention of serious crimes, or are you trying to say, or is Mr. Lukic trying to say that's not the case?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot try to tell you anything. We just read this item. It says quite clearly they participate in the detection and prevention of serious crimes, referring to theft or damage to arms, ammunition, combat equipment, mines and explosives and other types of serious property crime in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you're not trying to suggest, for example, that if you were aware that there was severe beating of individuals that that wouldn't involve your prevention, trying to prevent it, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you are suggesting that 7(A) would extend to that, Mr. Moore, there would appear to be some difficulties with the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will deal with it in generic terms if that's the easiest way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The language suggests a limitation to certain specific types of serious crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I accept that, and I'm curious actually about "just involve or include" but I can have things checked. I will deal with it in the generic way, if I may; probably the easiest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's set aside 7 for a moment. It is the duty of an officer of the security organ to prevent and detect serious crime along with other crimes. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the duty of every officer to prevent and report any criminal offences if he has any information about any criminal offences, and that includes, of course, the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That will do for my purpose. And then B: "The recommendation, regulation, organisation of security and self-protection measures, and also in other security matters organised and implemented by commands." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that all commands, all commanders at their respective levels, and all commanding officers, "komandiri," in their units shall deal with the question of the security and self-protection of their own unit and draft plans, of course according to their respective levels as well, for the men to be secure whilst discharging their tasks in the unit. The security organs participate and give guidelines for the drafting and proposing of such measures so -- in all the -- so that security would be -- would be at its best level in all units, installations, and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just turn the page to Article 46, please. I require your assistance on this. "Authorised officers of security organs have the right to use physical force for the purposes of overcoming resistance by a person who is to be taken into custody or for the purpose of repelling an attack against themselves or a person for whom they are providing security." Now, what I would like to know is who is an authorised officer?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, sir, this item 46 is most applicable in peacetime; namely, the powers of security organs in peacetime. Generally speaking, this entire regulations, these rules apply in peacetime. And in wartime and in a state of the imminent threat of war, they are restricted; these tasks are restricted. It is stated accurately here that all security organs may use firearms but the conditions are also specified, and it is specified under what conditions they can use them in contrast to other officers of the Yugoslav People's Army. And these officers were empowered to use such weaponry during peacetime, and it is regulated very precisely how it shall be used. But any organ of security would be severely punished if they used firearms contrary to all these very detailed regulations which are spelled out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So all security organs have the right to use firearms, as you have indicated. Let's just look below when they can use those firearms, shall we? "In carrying out tasks within their competence, authorised officers of security organs may use firearms only if they have no other way: A, protecting people's lives." Now, does that mean that, in actual fact, that if -- let's move on in time - if you were aware that people's lives were at risk, in a zone of responsibility, your zone of responsibility or indeed other zones of responsibility, and you were specifically told by your commander to go and sort the matter out, you would be entitled to use, I'm sure regrettably, firearms if you thought it was necessary to protect people's lives?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, Mr. Moore, let me try to repeat this. Once a security organ has used up all of their other powers - they're not stated here, IDing people, applying physical force, bringing people in - and they still can't deal -- or, rather, prevent what is described here from happening, then, well, it's quite clear, isn't it? Then firearms are resorted to. But it is certainly not the case that a security organ can resort to firearms right away before they've used up all their other powers under the rules, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. So if your charm doesn't work, if your persuasion doesn't work, and there's nothing left, you can use firearms. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about charm. I could warn them. If they still refuse, I could apply physical force. If I can overwhelm them by using physical force, then there's no need to use firearms. I'll just tie their hands behind their backs, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to move away from those regulations. I took a bit longer perhaps than I had hoped. Could we try and keep the answers a little shorter and I'll try and keep the questions a little shorter also. Can we look at tab 11, please, of this same document. So tab 11 is IDET, it's 06003051. And it is tab 12 for yourself. I want to deal with what I will call "notice." Now, have you got tab 12?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the security organ of the command of the 1st Military District, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you've already told us that you were kept in the loop in relation to various matters. Here is a document dated the 18th of October to the 1st Military District command security organ. What name do we put to that? Who is the person who is receiving this, 1st Military District command security organ?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the title itself tells you that this is a report sent to the security organ of the command of the 1st Military District. It was a rather large security organ in terms of pure numbers. I wasn't in touch with them at the time, but I think they were led by Major General Babic at the time; he was the chief. I do have to express some reservations as to the accuracy of this particular piece of information. I may have got the name wrong, but I think he was chief of security in the 1st Military District at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. The name, perhaps, is not so crucial but let's look at the content. A number of sources of the security organ of the JNA point to the fact that: "In the crisis area of the Republic of Croatia, particularly along the Sid-Negoslavci-Vukovar axis. There are a number of armed formations besides the JNA, primarily volunteer units which carry out combat activities and whose self-proclaimed commanders refuse to coordinate actions with the JNA units and are carrying out party propaganda activities through the residents, and particularly through local and foreign journalists, accusing the JNA, the leaders of the paramilitary compositions, are trying to mould themselves into heroes of the Serb people's resistance presenting their units as the nucleus of what appears to be ideological Serbian army, carrying out the activities under the parole of for the keen and the fatherland. Basically those are relatively small units of 20 or 30 men who, apart from mentioned, carry out other illegal activities. They are treating the prisoners of war brutally and increasingly often kill them on the spot and thus satisfy the justice. The abandoned houses are looted, and besides the money, jewellery and other precious items, in an organised manner they confiscate automobiles, tractors, and other mechanical devices, even cattle." It then goes on about smuggling. I won't go into any great detail of that. Now, on the English page, it's the second page, I'd like you to move on to the short paragraph that carries on: "Apart from this, an increasing number of instances of war looting." Have you got that? If you don't, I'll read it all and make it easy for you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the second passage, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Apart from this, an increasing number of instances of war looting are registered also by the volunteers and the TO headquarters." Then it goes on about a man called Bibic Milan tolerating even -- "tolerates and even organises the looting himself." It goes on about the selling off items. Then I want to start, please, with the paragraph commencing "lack of respect." Have you got that? "Lack of respect for the regulations."

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. "Lack of respect for the regulations, self-will, abusive positions and other are taking on troubling dimensions which doesn't bypass the members of the JNA." And then, for example, chief of security for the 453rd, gives a name. "While in the village of Negoslavci, illegally issued special authorisations to the civilians with which he helped them carry out a misuse. The authorised persons were then abusive to the citizens, even carrying out liquidations on occasions, on their own decisions. In order to overcome the registered weaknesses, and particularly to stop the genocide and the revenge-seeking, the anti-army activities and other crimes, it is necessary to place a bigger importance on these problems, and whenever possible, to document such activities in order to show it to the MUP and other organs of the Republic of Serbia. Pass on your information on the activities of the heads of the paramilitary formations and the anti-army and other criminal activities to the SSNO Federal Secretariat by the 25th." Now, here is a document that clearly refers to prisoners of war brutally and increasingly being treated, killing them on the spot, looting, even phrases like "genocide." This is a document, where did it go to? The 1st Military District? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Moore. It went to the 1st Military District. And what I can tell you is this: If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just before you start telling us, 1st Military District is OG South. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 1st Military District is the 1st Military District; it had jurisdiction over its own territory. If we see OG South as a temporary formation for the purpose of completing a very specific mission, which is liberating the Vukovar barracks and disarming the paramilitary units in and around Vukovar, in that case, you had units from the 1st Military District in that operations group, but the Guards Motorised Brigade was not a unit belonging to the 1st Military District. And -- could I perhaps explain this document, tell you what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sure you will be able to. But is Negoslavci not then the Guards Motorised Brigade zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the mission is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when we refer to the Sid-Negoslavci-Vukovar axis, does that not certain the Guards Motorised Brigade as well?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not. The Sid-Oriolik village -- Berak village axis was under the control of the Infantry Guards Division from the 1st Military District which had three Guards Brigades. One thing I wish to point out, and there seems to be some degree of confusion about that here, the Guards Brigade is called the Guards Motorised Brigade, whereas there seems to be a confusion of terms occurring quite frequently here. There is the 1st Guards Brigade, the 2nd Guards Brigade, the 3rd Guards Brigade. These are units of the Guards Division belonging to the 1st Military District. Therefore, if we talk about the Guards Motorised Brigade, there is no 1st or 2nd Brigade. Its name is the Guards Motorised Brigade and that name alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But in any event, this document requests for material to be sent to the SSNO. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, please, allow me to explain. This document was produced by the security administration based on my observations, based on the observations of security officers belonging to the Guards Motorised Brigade. If you've been listening carefully to my evidence, if you look carefully through my documents, you will have realised that I had reported on problems with Bibic Milan, Boro Bogunovic, this gentleman called Besic Muharem. All three of them were from the territorial jurisdiction of the 1st Military District. I was in no position to report to them. Instead, I was reporting to my own direct superior in terms of the technical line of command, my superior from the security organ, and he forwarded that to the security administration. The security administration is a technical body which now forwards this information to the security organ of the 1st Military District for measures to be taken and for checks to be run as to the veracity of what the organs of the Guards Motorised Brigade had been writing about. So there is that document for you. It's a very good thing you raised this point. Again, we worked in a systematic fashion, and we were struggling to preserve this country that was called Yugoslavia. And we didn't mind the fact that this man was a JNA security chief; we didn't look at that at all. We wanted steps to be taken against him also, if he indeed had been guilty of committing such errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say this document was produced by the security -- "by the security administration based on my observations," does that mean that references to the brutal treatment and killing of prisoner of war was known to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I explained that at the time, I, or rather my security organs -- I'm sorry, saying I, I, all the time; I'm speaking on their behalf. You have the sources stated specifically in any reports that I sent to the chief of the security administration. Such and such 6 captain misused his position of authority and took action on the ground that wasn't allowed. We wanted that to be checked, interviews to be conducted, and measures to be taken. He was not under our territorial jurisdiction. He was not within our competence at all, and there was absolutely nothing we could do about him or about what he did. Our duty, however, was to report on anything that we found out, which we duly did, and it was the competent -- the relevant bodies that were supposed to take any further measures. After that, I was not told again what exactly was done about this person, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking. I'm asking quite simply, there's a reference to treating of prisoners of war brutally and killing of them. And I am simply asking you: Did you have knowledge at that time that such actions were occurring? Simple question. Simple answer.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So a simple question requires a simple answer. And that would be: I remember reading that report, and we heard at the time about the sources used by those people who had provided our information. They said that a messenger had been killed. I don't have the report now to be able to check, but those people who were in possession of those certificates that this man had been issuing were treating the entire population in a disrespectful manner and we asked for that to be stopped. We did not track down any such individuals, but we wanted checks to be run in another area which was at the time under his control because the territory -- the area under his control was much larger than the one we were covering, the area under the control of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask the question one more time. Does that mean that you knew there was ill treatment and killing of prisoners of war? As you've said, you read this report.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I heard sources telling us about that. I forwarded a request for that to be verified or checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the phrase "genocide," refers to what, as far as you believed, as opposed to knew?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't produce this document. Whoever used that term "genocide," I really have no idea what they were referring to at the time. I can't be expected to interpret every single word that this person used. What I told you is what I knew. I told you about everything that I dispatched at the time and everything that I wrote about and everything that I'd shown you previously to this document being shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I wouldn't dream of trying to define genocide even as a lawyer. But genocide means specifically, does it not, the targeting of a certain group. In layman's language, that's what it means, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness has answered the question already. But the crux of my objection is Mr. Moore is now asking Mr. Sljivancanin to interpret the word "genocide," for him. And this word was suggested by whoever produced the document, and this person is a totally different person. Mr. Sljivancanin wrote about these facts but he never used the term. Mr. Moore can ask him what in very general terms he believes the word to mean, but he cannot possibly be asking him to interpret the term as used in this document or to suggest what the author of this document may or indeed may not have meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I think Mr. Moore has moved to agreeing with you the way he framed it at the end. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that "genocide" in everyday language means the targeting of a group. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, genocide is a dreadful thing. I wouldn't agree that it normally targets just one group, nor did I feel at the time that any acts of genocide had been committed in the area. I never used the term myself in any of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you're able to tell us that genocide is a dreadful thing, you obviously know, then, what it means by your definition. What does it mean, as you understand it, being a dreadful thing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on what I found out, based on what I learned, it means the extermination of a population in an area so that this population ceases to exist altogether. The cleansing of a population, the cleansing of an area from the entire population that used to inhabit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear it suggested that the JNA and the TOs who supported them were endeavouring to cleanse the area around Vukovar? Did you ever hear that dreadful thing being said?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anything like that being said. Wherever I was at the time, and which ever member of the JNA that I talked to or spent time with, whenever I was present, they were trying to treat every human being alike, and we wanted everybody to stay in that area as long as the right conditions were there. You say that the Territorial Defence men were supporting the JNA. That is, in fact, not true. They were not supporting us. They had their own tasks under the law that applied at the time for all the Territorial Defence forces to remain in the area. And I know that among the TO troops, there were people of all sorts of different ethnicities. They were not mono-ethnic. Some ethnicities were represented to a greater extent and some to a lesser, but they were certainly not a mono-ethnic force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I take it, then, having seen this document and the reference to revenge-seeking that you were aware or had notice that revenge-seeking was actually occurring?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never witnessed anything like that. I never witnessed any revenge-seeking or acts of revenge. When we arrived in the area, I tried, as I have explained already, to find out what had been going on before our arrival and to report all of that so that we might take measures to make sure that any such acts of revenge were foiled and to make sure that people understood the necessity to not do that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I take it, then, that you were aware, if not personal knowledge, but you were aware of the suggestion being made that there was revenge-seeking occurring?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please. [Interpretation] Can we just please have a more specific question, because the B/C/S interpretation that we're receiving, and I think that very much follows the English original, if then you were not aware personally, was a suggestion made to you. I'm not sure about the word where -- I think the phrasing of the question is not particularly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have said that you are not personally aware, but you'd been told about it, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be as accurate as possible. Again, I was not aware of any incident involving any acts of revenge. When we arrived in the area, there were all sorts of rumours circulating as to what had been going on before our arrival. Quite simply, clashes had erupted between the people living in the area. The term "revenge" was used. We wrote about everything that we had heard, and we tried to deal with this for as long as we were there. We took various measures to prevent this from happening. There was never a meeting at our command post without the commander pointing out that all the measures should be complied with and that the civilian population was to be treated in the most respectful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the word "revenge" had been used and inquiries had been made by you and that's what had been suggested, that people were taking the law into their own hands. That's right, isn't it? That's what you heard.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, whoever wrote this document used the words the way he used them. Again, we heard all sorts of rumours and stories about that when we arrived. Everybody was hoping that we would help them, and indeed, we did our best to oblige. From day one, after our arrival in the area, we did all we could to foil all rumours and to see whether there was any truth to the rumours and to restore order to the area to the extent that we were able to, as well as to disarm any disobedient individuals who could not comply with our requests, and for measures to be taken against them. I provided specific figures as to how many volunteers left our area on any given day, those undisciplined ones. Sometimes we would even send officers away. You have an example in my report. There was that officer who committed a disciplinary infraction. You have it quite clearly there what the commander had done about it and what we did about it. I can't give you any names right now, but one thing is certain we did take steps to stop such things from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it would be right to say that the ever-present fear of revenge was there when you were in Vukovar; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen, there's fighting. People are selling and buying weapons. People are arming themselves. Any psychopath can buy a weapon, someone you don't know. Well, of course there is fear. Secondly, people were moving about, moving out, returning. They would go of their own accord. The next day they want to go back. You have no idea what they are coming for. There is always fear. We weren't monsters not to feel any fear. Of course we felt fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's much more than that, Mr. Sljivancanin, isn't it? You were on the front line. What was happening was that people were being killed. They were being killed either by a Croat or a Serb, as they perceived it, and there was always the danger that revenge would reoccur or occur; isn't that right? It's equivalent to a civil war.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it, I've written it, and we've heard a great deal of evidence by a number of witnesses in this Court, starting with the peacetime period. There were acts of sabotage and people were killed. Later on, clashes erupted, regrettably. When the Guards Brigade arrived in the area, there was heavy fighting going on, armed clashes, fierce ones. In those days, I only knew of those who had been killed in combat, our own officers and soldiers as well as the soldiers belonging to the enemy forces. There were things like that happening. For example, my driver was killed. But I can't say that anyone killed him for any specific reasons, for revenge or anything like that. Someone killed him who was in a sheltered position, they just fired and they happened to kill my driver. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the situation as of the 18th of November changed because, for the first time, Croat defenders did not have their weapons. Many of them had disarmed themselves and they were extremely vulnerable to revenge attacks. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, I didn't feel that there was any sort of revenge-seeking in the air. I was concerned that some people might start flooding back who had long moved out of the area. And once they got wind of the fact that Vukovar had now been liberated, I was afraid that all these paramilitary formations would start flooding in to see what was going on. And then there is turmoil, and the situation gets out of hand. But I must say this too: I was pleasantly surprised to see those young soldiers and members of the TO in my presence, in the area where I was moving. And you saw that footage of the wounded being stretchered out of the hospital. It was the young soldiers doing that. And all the hospital staff was trying to get to the buses as soon as possible. So you can see for yourself they did everything within their power to help. Those people who had been through so much suffering, the people of that town, to try to show some sympathy, to help them through their pain, and to help them in any way they could and whatever they could. I really admired my soldiers. Those young people not infected by all the hatred, by all the revenge-seeking, not infected by anything that makes a man inhuman. I taught them what to do and how to behave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, who were they going to get the infection from?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the soldiers, most of the soldiers, the vast majority of soldiers and officers in the Guards Brigade did not feel any hate. We spoke earlier of how soldiers were selected. One spends sometimes growing up for 20 years, somebody that raises this person brings them, and now at the age of 20 they come to the JNA. We're not all alike. There may have been certain unstable individuals in a certain group infected by some sort of hatred, but I didn't notice that there were any such persons in my presence, but I'm not saying that there could not possibly have been also such individuals hiding or mimicry in a mass of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm back with us, Mr. Moore. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I make application for this document to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I move on, please, to tab 9.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit 847.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we move on, please, to tab 9 in the English version and tab 10 on the B/C/S version. The previous document was dated, I believe, the 18th of October. This is a document dated the 23rd of October; at least I hope it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got that document, Mr. Sljivancanin, it's tab 10?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just look at this document in fairly brief order, I hope. We can see the date is the 23rd of October. And it's, again, to the command of the 1st Military District sent by telegram under the heading "urgent." I just want to deal with various parts. I'm not going to read it. We would submit that the document is relevant for many issues, but trying to delineate them. Can we go to paragraph number 3 for a moment, please. It should read, it's on page 2: "Activities and occurrences which have a positive impact on the state of the morale in the division units." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And there are various headings, such as improving conditions of accommodation, food, expressing concern for the troops. And third from bottom, I just draw your attention to it, "Proper conduct towards prisoners." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we then move on to paragraph numbered 4 or titled four, really, "Activities or occurrences which have a negative impact on the state of the morale in the division units." There is reference to the statement of General Simovic. There is reference to spread of misinformation, about desertion and panic, invincible snipers, et cetera, about the enormous number of the enemy troops in the surrounding locations, particularly in Vukovar and Nustar. Thirdly, there's reference to a combat activities zone which needn't concern us. But just dealing then with the next topic, and we've already heard evidence about this. It starts: "In the village of Lovac." Do you see that? Have you got that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm following you. I have got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us just read it then, please. "In the village of Lovac, on one occasion, 80 villagers of Croatian nationality were captured by the TO Lovac and Dusan Silni detachment. They were then physically abused and four of the Lovac villagers were killed. "After the arrival of the Valjevo detachment in the village of Lovac, the captured villagers were used for clearing minefields and 17 villagers were killed. The wounded villagers were refused medical help by the staff at the Sid medical centre." Now, we have heard evidence, as I say, from the ECMM evidence about the village of Lovac. While clearly it is not within your zone of responsibility, it is right to say that you were aware of this incident at Lovac and the behaviour of the TO?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you, Mr. Moore, in relation to this document is this: It is true that it was sent to the command of the 1st Military District, the moral guidance department. That means that all the structures of the commands and units were dealing with prisoners of war on the ground and at the level of the brigade and of the division in this department, there were jurists, i.e., judges, who were to deal with many criminal complaints, reports, and such. I was familiarised with this document only when it was first read here in this courtroom, and I don't know anything about the content of this document, so anything that I was to tell you about it would be just interpreting what was meant by its author. I can just tell you that I was not familiar with it and I don't know anything about it. What I can see from this document is what I said before, that this refers to the units of the 1st Guards Motorised Division where there were the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Guards Infantry Brigades. I don't know what else I could tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But where was this sent to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this document was sent to the command of the 1st Military District to the moral guidance department, and it was sent by the commander for moral guidance in the 1st Infantry but then it is missing here but probably the division. The assistant commander for moral guidance of that division forwarded this document to the commander or perhaps Milan Jeremija was the deputy commander for instructions in matters of moral in some of the brigades within that division, but since I don't know the man, I can't tell you that with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is that there was a dreadful phrase, I'm sorry, but there was a track record, there was a history of abuses towards prisoners of war occurring at that time towards Croatian fighters and individuals who were not sympathetic to the JNA, and that was widely known. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully disagree with you. That may have existed in some instances, in some milieus, if people have reported about it. So it was in their own milieus. In the zone of the Guards Brigade, we did not have any such phenomena. There is also another document which I saw attached referring to the certificates which were issued by the security organs which we took from the residents and then we returned it to the security administration with proof about what that chief of security was doing, which was prior to our arrival. We sought to establish complete law and order in accordance with the law, and I don't know that any such cases happened in our zone. I'm not excluding that there may have been others elsewhere, but I wasn't aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, what you were saying is: Oh my goodness, the murder of 200-odd people at Ovcara came as a terrible surprise to you all. That's pretty much what you are saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a grievous crime to kill 200 people who were considered suspects for having committed criminal offences, and I was surprised, as a human being, that that should have happened. But it was not, I repeat, in the zone of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we'll look at what you did about it in due course. But let's look, please, at subdivider 8 and 9. This is document is well known, but nevertheless you should have the opportunity of looking at it. This is what's called the Zivota Panic warning document. It's Exhibit 415. Now, have you got the B/C/S version at subdivider or tab 8? Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where does this document come from?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comes from the command of the 1st Military District, the forward command post, and it is dated the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's right to say OG South are one of the nominated recipients. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to just deal with various aspects of it. I'll read it: "The Croatian armed forces are defeated in the area of combat operations carried out by the 1st Military District units. However, the war did not end with the fall of Vukovar and an even more fierce and brutal war against Ustasha forces is now ahead of it." It's my fault for not asking: Did you see and were you informed, or were you informed about this document by Panic by Colonel Mrksic? I should have asked that at the very start.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, seeing as that this document was drafted on the 18th of November, 1991, I would have to consult my war diary to see when it got in the command of the operations group and when it was filed there, but I have stated and I repeat: On the 18th, I attended a meeting with the commander in the morning. On the 18th, in the afternoon, on the 19th, on the 20th, and the 21st, I attended no meetings with the commander, if he conducted any, nor was I aware of any such meetings being held. And I saw this document for the first time when I arrived here at the court and when I was given this document. Never before did I have this document of the command of the 1st Military District, and it says here that it is addressed to the commander I chief [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Really, just a very easy question. You've seen this document many times. You know what the contents are. I am asking you a perfectly simple question: Did Mrksic tell you about this warning from Zivota Panic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we discussed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can we take it, then, that concerns expressed by Zivota Panic, and we're not talking actually concerns expressed, it was clear and unequivocal about the fears of what had happened and might happen. You're saying your commander never told you, because that clearly is something you would remember, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I have to say in responding to that: The 1st Military District has a wide zone. As far as I remember, at that time, it encompassed the zone of even somewhere there around the border towards Nis, then Vojvodina, Sarajevo, Banja Luka, and of course this area where Vukovar is, including the town of Osijek. So the commander, on the basis of all the data collected in his zone, writes such warnings. Now, if we link this to the document that we saw previously where this assistant commander for moral guidance wants the commander of the 1st Military District, that in the zone of the Guards Brigade there were some problems occurring, the commander sums up all the experiences coming from all the units in this document and then dispatches it to all units subordinated to him. But the shortcoming of this document in my view is its lack of precise information; what instances of negative behaviour are concerned, such as indicated in the document of the commander for morale saw that the commander, in this case Mr. Mrksic, would be informed -- yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I asked you very simply were you informed about the contents of this document by Mrksic? He had received a document from Zivota Panic saying that incidents had occurred and to be on your guard. Now, can we please forget about all the other areas where it's been, who it's going to. I am asking you a very simple question. Can we please, once again, have a very simple answer: Were you aware of that information being imparted to you, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say I don't remember having seen this document ever before, that is to say, until I arrived here at The Hague. But let me add: The commander may have received this document if it is filed in the war diary, and he assessed that in the zone -- that he was commander of, there were no such practices, such occurrences, and that also there was no need for him to inform everybody. That is perhaps why I don't know anything about it, in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you're saying you don't know anything about it. Is that what you're actually saying? We've gone around in this enormous speech, but what you say is this is perhaps why I don't know anything about it. I'm not talking about the document; I'm talking about the contents. Are you saying you don't know about the Zivota Panic warning?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I knew nothing about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that there is an entry in the Guards war diary of the 19th of November of its receipt at 6.00 in the morning, or the entry is at 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is an entry, it was certainly received at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you never check the war diary to see what was happening as a security organ?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never checked the war diary. The Chief of Staff had the right to check the war diary and to control what was being entered in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So whether, in actual fact, things had happened in the zone of responsibility of OG South or whoever it is, you say you weren't informed of the content of this? That's the bottom line, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is an equivocal question. If that refers to this document, I assert that I have never seen this document prior to coming to The Hague. Now, what happened in the zone of the Guards Brigade is something that I always sought to be informed about. And to give you a very brief answer, in that period, of course that is a subject for some analysis, I was not interested in the zone of Jakubovci, Ovcara, et cetera, because that was not the zone of combat operation. That was an area where units rested. There may have been infiltrations but -- by terrorist groups, and there were such instances, or a mortar fire could have been opened on units, but there were no combat operations proper there. And I moved in the area where there were combat actions and where barracks were to be deblocked and the paramilitary units disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, it's not an equivocal question, it is decision time. Either Mr. Mrksic told you or he didn't. Now what is the answer?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Told me what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "That every unit must fully control the situation on the territory of its area of responsibility, commanders at all levels will be responsible for this. Wartime laws have not entered into force, and therefore, as always, nobody has the right to retribution and other kinds of revenge which some local TO, Territorial Defence units carried out. In future, arrest those who commit any such acts and undertake appropriate legal measures." It cannot be clearer. It cannot be more specific. It drives specifically at your function and the protection of individuals, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, Mrksic issued such tasks almost on a daily basis.
