In looking through these documents in preparing myself for the testimony, I remember the number of document issued by Mrksic as strictly confidential 250-1. That was an order that he issued in October. And concretely speaking, as far as this document is concerned, I was only informed of it when I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have asked you: Did you -- or were you told by Mrksic about this Zivota Panic warning? This is after the fall of Vukovar. That's the importance of it. Now did he or did he not tell you the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already replied to that question. I was familiarised with this here document only when I arrived at The Hague. And I did not attend any meetings, probably held by Mrksic. So on the 19th in the evening, if this document came on the 19th, I was not at that meeting and I had not seen -- I did not see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you were not told of this document. Is that what you're also trying to say?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was not familiarised with this document. I did not specifically discuss the document, any document with Mrksic, including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to other parts of this document. I'm sorry it was my fault for not asking it in correct sequence. "The Croatian armed forces are defeated in the area of combat operations carried out by 1st Military District units. However, the war did not end with the fall of Vukovar and even more fierce and brutal war against Ustasha forces is now against us." It goes on about Ustasha forces and especially their more extreme members will continue to fight subversively. And then goes on by saying: "By carrying out sabotage and terrorist actions just behind our lines as well as deeper in our territory and liberated parts." Would you consider that that is an accurate analysis of what commanders were considering at that time after the fall of Vukovar? It is really the first step on a number of battles yet to come?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I can hardly be expected to interpret what the author of this document meant. Here is what he wrote. Again, I wasn't familiar with this document. I don't know what he was planning or what battles would ensue. I really don't know and I can hardly be expected to interpret his thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 refers to Geneva Conventions and prisoners of war. Paragraph 5, I'd like to deal with, please. "During preparations on the 19th of November." Do you see that? Have you got that section?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "During preparations on the 19th of November, 1991, most resolutely prevent any disobedience, unsoldierly appearance, and behaviour. Commanders of all levels will ensure realistic and favourable conditions for this task to be accomplished." As far as you're aware, would that apply to military units within OG South, as a general term, or a general category?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that I'm looking at this, now that I'm listening to you read this, this is a general assignment and this is something that was copied from the military rules. This just adds more emphasis to the task that we, as members of the Guards Brigade, were always familiar with. This was an ongoing task for all units to remain disciplined. The fact that the commander here seems to be emphasising the need for discipline probably means that it was an issue of particular importance for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You as an officer, not just security organ, you as an officer, would it be right to say, have a duty to ensure that disobedience, not perhaps overly concerned about unsoldierly appearance, and behaviour, is an important directive?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That applies to every army, including the JNA. Discipline was the foundation, the cornerstone of any task. But believe me, even in peacetime conditions, when soldiers are peacefully in their barracks, you can't do everything fully. In a situation like this where you had inter-ethnic clashes, it was very difficult to keep it all spick and span, so to speak, down to the last detail. We, the officers, did our best to make sure that discipline was sufficient and did everything within our power to ensure that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Kindly tell the Court, then, what it was that you did to ensure that the attacks upon the buses was either prevented or punished? And when I say that, I'm -- in relation to the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never even assumed that the buses would come under attack. Everything I did, that was within my power, I did to help my assistant who was taking those buses into barracks. I told him that he should have a sufficient number of men with him to make sure those people wouldn't be hurt or jeopardised. He told me that back at the barracks there were the most responsible officers who were responsible for discipline there, and he told me that there was a military police company present there. Therefore, I believed that all the appropriate steps would be taken. If the chief of security alone could take care of everything, well, there would be no need for any other officers, would there. The barracks at the time for me was a safe facility where people could go about their tasks as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But yesterday I asked you specifically about the personal responsibility of an officer to go and see what was happening, and indeed you gave us an enormous explanation about how desirable it was for personal involvement of a commander. Now, I'm asking you: What did you actually do? You've told us that you were told by Vukasinovic that everything was there. What did you do? Did you check? Did you radio? Did you go personally? I'd like to know what you did.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As chief of security, I had no power to issue any orders or, indeed, to control the work of my superiors. When Vukasinovic informed me that there had been attempts, such as verbal taunts or attempts at mistreating those 24 persons that, pursuant to my order, he was to return to the hospital -- or pursuant to my request, if you like, I then asked him which officers are there at the barracks? When I heard about this happening. He said there was Lieutenant-Colonel Panic, Lieutenant-Colonel Lukic, Captain Predojevic, and he mentioned a couple of other military police officers. That was my personal belief at the time, knowing those officers and knowing what the overall situation was that those officers would take all the necessary measures to prevent that. It wasn't my function or my role to supervise their work. Had they not been there, I would have gone myself to see what was going on. Since I had been informed that they were there, I felt there was no need for me to go As for what you asked me yesterday, you asked me specifically what I would have done if I had been the brigade commander and if I had issued a task to an officer, how would I have checked whether the task had been carried out successfully, and that was the answer -- that was the question that I answered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you remember yesterday in your evidence you told us that you wandered about, walked about, I should say, with a radio - do you remember that - "at all times"? Did you ever use your radio to try and find out what was happening at the barracks, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no radio link to the barracks. I had a radio link to my command post back at Negoslavci and the command at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, attempt, by radio, to find out what was going on at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Why? Because I had been informed by my assistant. He told me which of the officers were at the barracks at the time, and I believed that order and discipline reigned supreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you told us yesterday that it was prudent and wise to ensure that one kept an eye, a constant eye on what was happening. Why did you not use the radio? Why did you not try and find out if things had changed?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a specific question yesterday, what would I have done as commander in relation to a specific mission? And this question now, I'm telling you this: The officers who were at the barracks, they were from the command structure of the Guards Brigade. I was not their superior. I put my trust in them. Those were officers I knew. I believed that they would do their job in a soldierly way. I believed since they were there, there was no need for me to go and supervise them, nor, indeed, was that my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer is you didn't do anything; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the answer is not I didn't do anything. The answer is what I just told you. If you like the answer you're providing yourself better, well, you can keep it. My answer is what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move to tab 25, please. It's a 65 ter document, 1D0038, and it should be dated the 16th of October. English version, 25. Well, this is certainly a document you have seen because you wrote it, or compiled it, perhaps, is a better phrase.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two documents here, the 6th of October, that is tab 27 in my folder. I'm not sure if I'm looking at the right one. The brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's all right, don't worry about it. Would you go to tab 26, and we are on tab 25. Let me make sure that that's -- I'm certainly right for that. 26.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now that is a document created by yourself, Guards Motorised Brigade, 16th of October, 1991, Negoslavci, urgent to SSNO. You've got that. Let us just deal with it in part. If we move down to the principal paragraph, it reads as follows --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just finding out what certain initials meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "The work of the security organ and the military police mostly focuses on the following: The security organ units mostly detect indications and prevent instances of individual or group defeatism in the units in the area of combat operations. Look for ZNG, National Guard Corps, and MUP sources in the general area of the brigade's command post and the rear command post. Detect, arrest, and close channels used by the MUP and ZNG, members to infiltrate the Vukovar area who may be infiltrated in the area of the command post Negoslavci village and further afield for various reasons. After an evaluation is made of the whole territory where combat operations are carried out, observe persons for whom there is a previous information of indicative behaviour. Organise and introduce special war security regimes in the general area of combat operations, and offer professional and other assistance to members of the Negoslavci Secretariat of the Interior and the TO Defence staff." Do you remember this phrase I've used about "eyes and ears." But this is quite simply you saying what your function and tasks are, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Moore please slow down slightly when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it, Mr. Sljivancanin? You are stating here what your function and tasks are.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the interpretation I got may be different from what you've read out. It places me squarely in a dilemma, because the interpretation is not what this reads. So I showed you yesterday that document from the chief of security of the cabinet and the security administration requesting the command of the Guards Brigade, or, rather, its chief of security to urgently submit to them a working map showing the involvement of security organs and military police units of the Guards Motorised Brigade. They were the tactical, focal point for providing equipment to these units with any special equipment, so that in cooperation with other focal points, they could supply this equipment, bring the manpower levels up, and do whatever was necessary for those units. It was based on that request that I tried, in this document, to tell them where these respective units were involved and what they were doing. It says "security organs of the unit," and reference here is to the Guards Brigade. It says in the title "the Guards Brigade command," and that's where the interpretation was different; that's why I'm saying this. Principally they were involved in these tasks stated here. Further down are the exact locations for the military police units and described their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, that's an enormously long answer. But the reality is you're looking for ZNG and MUP forces. That's right, isn't it? You say it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were looking for members and particularly leaders of the ZNG units and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, that you were looking for names?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was looking for people who were the organisers of that armed insurgency. I didn't know some of the names. I learned some of the names in the area or by listening to their radio frequencies, and I was given some names by my superior security organs. I don't know how they'd got hold of the names to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you were looking for names. You were looking for the names of the people who were organising the resistance against you. That is right, isn't it? It's not a particularly difficult point, is it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not -- I was looking for names, I was looking for specific people, specific person who were the organisers of this armed insurgency. For example, I was looking for Mile Dedakovic in order to meet him. I'm not sure what you mean when you say I was looking for names. I was looking for specific persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, it's not a case of army, and it's not a case of law, it's a question of common sense. You are security organ. You have got various sources, and it is like a jigsaw. You put together the pieces, and you find out who are the people who are in charge, who are the people who are politically active, who are the people militarily active. You don't know that until you are either told it or given it by someone. That's right, isn't it? And names will crop up from various sources. It's not rocket science, is it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough. All right. I understand now. I did not know the names of all the leaders of this armed insurgency because they used code-names or aliases. I was looking for those persons. But I did not wish to be played because someone might have planted the wrong person on me with no documents whatsoever, and this turned out to be the wrong person, not the person I was after. I personally in the security organs were looking primarily for the leaders of the paramilitary units, the ZNG and the MUP, those who had organised the armed insurgency in Vukovar, in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not just political opposition, it's also military leadership as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. But we were looking at military leaders too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, just a question of common sense, lists were being kept of the people who were the leaders. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got some of the names of those people who were the leaders of this all from the technical bodies in the security organ, and I got some of the names from the civilians, those leaving their cellars. I got some of the names during interviews with these civilians. I got some of the names from individuals who had been captured during the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I'm saying: Lists were compiled of the people. You just have to keep a record of who you're being told. It's not all going down in memory, is it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. We kept lists and we tried to take down as many names as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just move on to this document. Reading on: "In addition, the security organ are engaged in the operative team that works with prisoner of war, determines who took part in the commission of crimes, and identifies the ZNG and MUP leaders in Vukovar." So you were basically trying to ascertain who was doing what on the other side; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you just assist me with one little phrase in this document? Because when one looks at the next line, it says as follows: "Furthermore, the chief of the security organ is engaged in the command of the Operations Group South on planning combat operations and providing assistance to the units on the front line." Now, who is the chief of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said it before, haven't I? I am the chief of the security organ. I wrote this when the commander took the decision. As far as I remember, every time a decision was taken, in some way I was involved or I was there, or at least I was at the command post to hear what the decision was in relation to any units, especially those belonging to the Guards Motorised Brigade. If you go through the documents very carefully, the decisions and orders issued by the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sljivancanin, I'm just dealing with this document. You say that you are the chief of the security organ. But look at the following passage: "... in the command of the Operations Group South." It's not referenced just to Guards Motorised Brigade, is it? It's OG South.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you interrupted me, but that's just what I was about to explain. Commander Mrksic, as commander of the Guards Brigade, took the decision to have the Guards Motorised Brigade units involved in lifting the siege of the barracks and in disarming the paramilitary units. In addition to this, he gave other units certain tasks briefly that were outside the Vukovar area and were not involved in the tasks being carried out in Vukovar itself, if that's what we mean when we say "operations group." I don't see any other unit with the exception of the Guards Brigade that was involved, and he gave these tasks to battalions, the 1st and the 2nd Motorised Battalion, the 1st and the 2nd Military Police Battalions, and that's what I accepted it to be. And that's what my understanding was when I was actually there, and I was physically present when these decisions were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What you are trying to say to this Court is that you are the chief of the security organ only for the Guards Motorised Brigade but not OG South. That's what you're saying, isn't it, in simple terms?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding. That's how it was. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, see if you can help me on this topic. You have OG South, what I will call an umbrella command. You are the security organ for one of the brigades, the Guards Motorised Brigade. Am I correct so far?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And underneath, as it seems to be the case, there were other brigades subsumed under the OG South command; do you agree with that? 80th is one of those examples.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade had the level of a Guards Brigade, and quite a strong one. You could perhaps have assumed that Colonel Mrksic was our superior in relation to a superior task in as far as the brigade was involved in that particular area, but there was no such thing as a separate OG South command. Once Colonel Bojat and Ljubicic had left the area, all that remained was the command of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, in the British army, you normally have three brigades sitting within a division. Could you just switch off -- move the microphone as it's rather like a North Sea gale at the moment. Thank you very much. You have various brigades, each brigade will be represented by a security organ, the chief of the security organ for that brigade; that's right. You were for the Guards Motorised Brigade. Who was for the 80th? Who was your equivalent?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 80th -- the man actually gave evidence here. I just met him once, no more than once in Vukovar, Dragi Vukosavljevic, that's him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, then, who was actually the definitive commander of the security organ to assist Mrksic? Who were you reporting up to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no commander in a security organ. There is the chief and there are security clerks, desk officers. I was subordinated to the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade, as chief of security, to Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I want to know who the chief of the security organ was for OG South; otherwise, the way you're explaining it, Mrksic is going to have to speak to the security organ for each and every brigade. And I'm suggesting what Mrksic did perfectly reasonably was he made you chief of the security organ for OG South. He had one person to link with. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that OG South, if that's what we assume it to have been like. This is a temporary unit for a particular mission. This group does not have any permanent command. It does not have an establishment command. You can set one up. If that is established, there should be a written order for establishing that command that specifies all its members. If there is no such order, then there's no command; at least that's how I see it. I never received such an order like that. I know that I was chief of security of the Guards Brigade. Mrksic, in his capacity as commander, was never supposed to talk to any chief of security of any of the other brigades, the 80th, for example. He would always talk to the commander of that brigade. The chief of security has the duty to inform the brigade commander about everything that he knows. He works for the brigade, not for anybody else's purposes or needs or for a different chain of command. He only works for that particular unit. In the JNA, there was no dual command. Please try to understand that. There was singleness of command and there was unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I do understand it. All I'm simply suggesting to you is that in actual fact, even though it may well have been a temporary unit, nevertheless it had to have an inherent structure where there was a single point person for the security organ, i.e., the chief of the security organ, and that was you, whether you like it or whether you don't.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the arbitrary positions on your part. I was issued no such orders and if there is such an order, I should like to see it and then I shall apologise for everything that I'm saying because I would be remiss for not having familiarised myself with that. On the other hand, I believe that there's a mistake on the part of the 1st Military District for not having issued such an order. Had I been the chief of security of OG South, and had a command like that existed, I would have been invited for a meeting with the commander, with the chief of the 1st Military District to be informed of that, and I would not be receiving information from the chief of security of the cabinet of the federal secretary, but I would have been given information from the chief of security of the 1st Military District. So if any such document exists, please present it -- exists, present it to me and I shall apologise for everything that I have said. I cannot speak about things that I know nothing about. I'm trying to be very sincere in providing my answers, and you can see whether they are acceptable to you or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then, let's look at it another way. When was OG South set up with Mrksic in charge?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a record of that, an entry in the war diary, namely that Commander Mrksic assumed the post of commander of the OG sometime in October. Whether it was on the 8th, or 9th, or 10th of October, I'm not sure. I've said that I attended no such meeting nor any change-over in that respect. Now what was said to him and whether he has a written order and what specific tasks he was given, I don't really know; namely, I never discussed that with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer is 8th, 9th, 10th of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic has a concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction of the transcript, page 60, line 11, there should be a separation between the answer and the question in line 11 from the words of "there is a record of that," which is actually the beginning of Mr. Sljivancanin's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before you go any further, Mr. Sljivancanin, I've got 19 lines of answer to deal with. Can I just try and deal with that and then perhaps we can move on. But we've got the 8th, 9th, 10th of October. When the OG command was being set up, it ceased on the 24th, there or thereabouts, of November, so it's clearly a temporary command for the duration of the battle of Vukovar. Would that be, in very general terms, correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not fully accept what you've just said. I believe, and from what I learned from military regulations and rules, if a temporary command is set up for a specific mission, and if no order has been issued spelling out precisely the period from which -- to which the command shall function, in my view, that command shall cease to exist once the mission has been accomplished, and that mission was accomplished, completed on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You knew Mrksic before coming to Vukovar. You knew him pretty well, actually; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right either. I met Mr. Mrksic for the first time, I believe, some three years before the Vukovar event. But don't take my word for it. He was, however, never my immediate superior. He was my superior officer when he became the commander of the brigade, and in August 1992 I met Mrksic as my first immediate commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's 1991. But the point I want to make --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1991. That's right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not at all. It's not a problem. But the question I want to ask is this: Didn't it occur to you on the 8th, 9th, 10th of October, seeing that there were going to be security organs for each brigade, that it was desirable for there to be a security organ, a chief of security of security organ for OG South to coordinate such material?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, it was my idea, my position, and it still is that that was not necessary because it was an entering command, the mission was a temporary one, and the security organs, once they immediately applied themselves to that kind of a mission, they should concentrate on that particular task without having the possibility of dealing with other elements, the development of a network of contacts, the training of personnel, the collection of data, the manning of units, but they should focus primarily on the discharge of the concretely issued task. That is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you never said to Mrksic at any time that it might be desirable or something that should be thought about? The answer, I presume, is no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never discussed the subject with Mrksic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you explain a piece of evidence that was given by Vukosavljevic who said that when he went to report, he, being in charge of the 80th, the security organ of the 80th, that he reported to Karan and Vukasinovic who were your subordinates? Can you explain that to the Court how that was occurring, if you weren't in charge of OG South?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Moore, I don't exactly remember that that is what Mr. Vukosavljevic precisely said, but I can give you an explanation if you are interested. Because of security considerations, namely when the 453rd Brigade was there, I tried to get in touch with the security organ, and he told me I have my own commander so he had no document which actually instructed him and joined upon him to provide me with any information. When the 20th Partisan Brigade was there, I saw the commander of that brigade several times, I've said for which reasons, and he told me that he knew everything in his own brigade and he was managing things and informing Mrksic, reporting to Mrksic about the situation in his brigade and he was not, of course, participating in any combat operations in the area of Grabovo. When the 80th Motorised Brigade came to the area - that may have been on the 18th, I'm not quite sure of the date - my assistant for counter-intelligence work told me that a new security organ that had appeared on that territory had reported and he told me what his name was, and he told me that this was a good man who had expressed the desire to cooperate with us and to exchange information if any of it was relevant and significant to us. Then I said all right, I should see this man if he wants to cooperate with us. So one evening he came to us, and I asked him to whom was he submitting reports and to whom was he reporting, and he told me that he was submitting his reports to the command, to the chief of security of his own corps, that he knew what his tasks were, and that he was prepared to cooperate with us if there should be any need in order for us to exchange important information, information important to us. In that period, the plan was for that brigade to remain in the combat operations zone and our further -- any traces of our further cooperation and action in concert was lost. I never saw him again. He worked according to instructions from his commander. We were exhausted, we were on the first line of battle, and we waited -- could hardly wait for someone to come and replace us. And perhaps this rotation of units is the reason why concentration should falter and people, perhaps, don't remember everything in detail. But neither Vukasinovic or Karan ever told me that he had submitted any written reports to them, nor any report for that matter. Those people will be giving evidence here themselves, so you can also ask them that question. But as far as I know, they told me that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer is you weren't aware of that? It's taken you 32 lines.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I had to explain accurately. I want to tell the truth. If you want me to just say yes or no all the time, it will be some sort of a quiz show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a general remark that Mr. Moore is extracting this conclusion, which he just gave us, from his sentence that he was not familiar with it; whereas Mr. Sljivancanin has clearly explained his position in regard to the thesis advanced by Mr. Moore, namely to what Mr. Moore said, Vukosavljevic had stated. So that I believe it would be very expedient if we were indicated the mark on the page where Vukosavljevic stated what Mr. Moore says he had stated because I believe it was somewhat different. But if Mr. Moore asserts that Mr. Vukosavljevic stated that he had reported to Karan and this other person, that has to be shown by a precise indication of the page in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will endeavour to do so. I'm just having checks made on a transcript reference. In any event, I want to move on to another document, if I may, please, and I will come back to that if it assists. Or Your Honour can allow me two or three minutes to locate the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Moore. It will be checked by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm told -- well, would Your Honour give me a moment. It's perhaps just best to deal with it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could we go back to -- it's the page reference 8697, line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I read as follows, it's a question by Mr. Domazet: "This is what I'm talking about, the security line, the professional line, not the chain of command which is completely clear to all of us, I'm talking about the line of the security organ that is very special in its work, and if we're talking about that line, I would like to know when you arrived in Negoslavci and when you were involved in Operation Vukovar. Who was it who gave you instructions, orders, along that line? Who did you cooperate with directly? "A. To the Prosecutor's question, I've already spoken about that and I informed the Trial Chamber about that. Around the 10th, the brigade command told me that the brigade command was subordinated to the Guards Motorised Brigade. In other words, that the Guards Motorised Brigade is also the command of the OG South, and according to the rules of service a subordinated security organ has to report to his superior security organ in the command. I went to the command post of the Guards Motorised Brigade and in -- and I found Captain First Class Karan with whom I had the initial conversation that concerned our profession." That deals with Karan. May I deal, then, with, I believe it's 8702, line 16. "Mr. Domazet: There seems to have been -- "Judge Parker: It reads as follows on line 9, 8702: It indicates that the chief of security of the 80th brigade was Colonel Sljivancanin. Is that the answer that was given? Is that correct?" Well, clearly it's not correct. "Mr. Domazet: No, no, this is a mistake. "The Witness: If you're asking me, no, no, of course not. I was the chief security of the 80th Brigade, and the colonel was the chief of security of the Guards Motorised Brigade and also the chief of security of OG South." I will try and find the other reference to Vukasinovic. There is a clear reference to Karan, and there is a clear reference to the fact that he said that his unit, the 80th, was subordinated to the Guards Motorised Brigade security organ; isn't that right? That he contacted Karan on that basis?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to you reading this and my comment is this: Mr. Vukasinovic is not sufficiently professionally acquainted with military rules. Never can a brigade be subordinated to another brigade. Where he said that the 80th Brigade was subordinated to the Guards Brigade, I have never heard of anything of the kind. And I believe, and there is no such order that the command of the Guards Brigade was the command of the OG South, as he said it, and I adhere to my position. I can only say that this was an interpretation of his -- the way he saw things, but this has to be proved by documents, to see whether that is indeed true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another document. Document 20, tab 29. Would Your Honour forgive me. Your Honour, I'm informed that I have not tendered this document as an exhibit. Could I ask for it to be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 848.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Am I correct in assuming you deliberately did not tender one earlier document, that was number 9? I think the witness said he knew nothing of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Will Your Honour just allow me a moment. No, I did not deliberately not tender it. It is my error for not doing so. I am told, a whisper from the side, that it is actually an exhibit anyway. It's Exhibit 636 as shown on the index that we have supplied at tab 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you now just a general question before we move on to other documents. You say you're here to tell the truth and to try and assist everyone. Would you consider, and did you consider, at that time, that Mrksic was a commander who was weak in certain aspects of his character?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not Mrksic's superior to be able to keep detailed tabs on how he was discharging his tasks. I may have disagreed with some positions of his or perhaps I might have had a different opinion as to how something was to have been gone about. Every person, every man has his own method of work. I may have thought that Mrksic, in certain instances, should have been stricter with some of his subordinate officers and then again I may not have been right, and maybe I was wrong when I thought that he should have been stricter in discharging some task with his units, and perhaps he was right and wanted to do it his way whilst abiding by the rules and regulations. But I never thought that Mrksic was a weak commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The reason why I ask you is because on tab 29 and tab 30. I want to deal with a document of the 10th of December which is your re-evaluation. I seem to remember, even though it's dated the 10th of December, you say you compiled it, I think, on the 21st of November. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, which I see before me, was compiled by me in December, and as indicated on the date it bears, the 10th of December, it was sent to the security administration. And on the 21st of November, I had sent a report from Vukovar, just like I had sent earlier reports on the events that were unfolding in the zone of the Guards Brigade. But that is a different report, not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So this is your document compiled by yourself, compiled on the 21st, sent on the 10th of December. I see Mr. Lukic nodding, no, vigorously. Can you repeat it, then.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I'm saying, Mr. Moore. On the 21st of November, having accomplished our tasks, and after everything that I told you about had transpired, I, as the chief of security, compiled the report which, as a report that I regularly sent from the zone of combat operations and I sent it to the chief of security in the cabinet of the federal secretary and to the security administration. This document which is now before us, I compiled after my talk with the General Aca Vasiljevic in the security administration on the 10th of December, and I dispatched it on the 10th of December to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for that. Let us then deal with -- we can see it's your signature, we can see the date, and we can see who it's going to, and the progress -- the progress combat operations conducted to liberate Vukovar. I want to deal with the first part. "The Guards Motorised Brigade commenced executing its combat task in very specific and difficult conditions. The Guards Motorised Brigade commander, Mr. Mrksic, continually emphasised the unit's ability to execute the most difficult of tasks, but when he was assigned an actual combat task he started vacillating." Now, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not what I meant, it is clearly written. If you go on to read this, there were some doubts, some officers were saying that there was treason in the military leadership. Actually, I would rather say that there was vacillation on the part of some officers because of their fear from action, and that is what I put down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'd suggest that's not what it seems to suggest. Reading on, and I will not mention one of the names because it's a protected

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: traitors at the top of the military, as he said, should be replaced, thinking primarily of army General Kadijevic, and that he would start on the execution of the task after that had been settled." Now, that's, I'd suggest, is fairly clear. Are you saying, then, that Mrksic was suggesting that the traitors at the top, Kadijevic, was, in his terms, the problem, a traitor at the top, let's remove Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually put that down in this report. That is the kind of information that I heard at the time; namely, that there was suspicions to the effect that General Kadijevic was a traitor, and among him were a part of the military top leadership. It was suggested to me that I was supporting General Kadijevic. Then I said to Mrksic that this was misinformation that he was dealing with, that I knew General Kadijevic personally, and that I was firmly of the view that he was a Yugoslav-oriented and committed person and that I was convinced that these stories were untrue, and that as long as my men were providing security for General Kadijevic, not a hair from his head would fall. After that, Mrksic went for a talk with General Kadijevic together with Aca Vasiljevic, Blagoje Adzic, and I am not sure whether any other general was there, Colonel Vuk Obradovic was. I don't know what the subject of their conversation was, but I do know that this was not a putch [as interpreted], as many of the media portrayed it, and as was said by General Aca Vasiljevic in an interview granted the Nin magazine in 1992, because he had been at that meeting with General Kadijevic. I wrote that this was similar because it was prior -- immediately prior to the brigades going to discharge this mission. This was not in July, this was on that day, immediately prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I considered that this document was not on the screen. I looked at various screens around me and I didn't see it. There is a name mentioned on it which is a protected witness. If -- if it is being shown outside, then regrettably, it will have to be redacted. I thought that it was not on the screen. I must say, I thought people were using hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will learn the answer to that. It has not been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now when it comes to a convenient moment, we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm almost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, you can see that there are various names mentioned there. I don't want to repeat them because one of them, as I say, is a protected witness. But what you say is you mention those individuals and said, Mr. Mrksic: "He found people of similar views to his." So the view that you took was that Mrksic, himself, was unhappy about Kadijevic, that he talked hard and vacillated when it came to combat, and he had people who basically supported his position. That's what that means, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's what it means. As chief of security, was supposed to know what the situation was in the brigade. Mrksic listened to all the various positions held by these different officers and I tried to dissuade him, I tried to make himself see that this was a lie. It is from this witness stand that I now wish to address the public and everyone to say that I knew General Veljko Kadijevic's family very well. I knew his brothers too. They were pro-Yugoslav, particularly General Kadijevic. That was certainly my impression, and this is what I told Colonel Mrksic at the time. Had Mrksic been hatching any plans, I don't think General Kadijevic would have agreed to see him to begin with. Now, what exactly did they talk about, Vuk Obradovic, Blagoje Adzic, and Aca Vasiljevic, Mrksic, and Veljko Kadijevic, well, only they can say because I wasn't there. I didn't attend the meeting. But I heard these positions that were taken from Mrksic, and I informed both Vuk Obradovic and the chef du cabinet of the federal secretary to whom I was subordinate. I also assigned extra security just to cover all the eventualities and for the measures to be what they were supposed to be. These people that I told you about, they had talks immediately that evening, and I have no idea what the substance of that talk was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with this matter very quickly if I can, please. It's taking a long time this morning. But the situation was Mrksic went to see Kadijevic, Kadijevic remained in power, and isn't it right that there has often been said that the Guards Motorised Brigade was sent to Vukovar as a punishment because of its insubordinate approach with Mrksic at the helm? Hasn't that been said?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, this is misinformation, pure and simple. And this, in relation to these people - I'm going mention some of them - Kavalic, there, he was one of these people spreading misinformation out of fear. The day before this happened, the brigade had already received orders for resubordination to the 1st Military District and it was off on a mission. This is a decision that had been taken previously. There was no need for anyone to take a new decision now. As I said, it was supposed to have been of a day earlier, had not all of this happened. That's why I believe this to be misinformation. People who arbitrarily tried to spread word through the public media as well about things that were simply untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that Mrksic went to Vukovar with a question mark over his career from the powers that be, and that he is an extremely and was an extremely ambitious officer at that time. Now it's really two questions. Do you accept that he went, along with others, with question marks over their career and their commitment to the cause?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I totally disagree. If you want to look at it that way, Mrksic was promoted to the rank of general by General Kadijevic, of all people. He was on an upward grade, so to speak, and he was promoted several times over the following years. He had a brilliant military career. He became the number two person in the General Staff, if I can put it that way, the head of the land force. It is not true that Mrksic's career was hamstrung. Quite the opposite in fact, he made progress all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would suggest to you that Mrksic's career was built on the rubble of Vukovar. That's why he was promoted the way he was.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that either. Mrksic got the rank of general after Vukovar; that much is true. A decision was taken by his superiors, he had the requisite training, and everything else. And probably he proved his mettle in a number of other positions later on, because new people came to some of the leading positions in the armed forces. And I don't think he would have been promoted on the strength of Vukovar alone. He probably had other qualities too. I was never his superior, I never worked directly with him. I don't know about he went about performing his job, and it is simply impossible for me to assess that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Over the break, Mr. Moore, could you just confirm whether document at tab 29 is, in fact, Exhibit 843?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've got it down as 843. Did I not call it that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not so described in your index sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's because the index was done before it was made an exhibit. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume just a little after 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to go through the documents at a greater rate than we're going, Mr. Sljivancanin, and if you could keep your answers is little shorter, I would be very grateful. Can I ask you, please, to go to the fifth main paragraph of tab 29. It should read: "A few days after the conduct of combat operations began ..." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to deal with one or two matters on this paragraph and two or three other paragraphs. "A decision was issued for the Guards Motorised Brigade commander to take over the OG South command." So we have, quite clearly, in this document, that reference, you now have accepted it. We move on down that paragraph, and you refer to: "The greatest difficulty was with the Podunavlje Brigade where I personally had to send two battalions who wished to leave their positions back to those positions." I'm curious about the phrase "where I personally had to send," bearing in mind you are a gentleman who says that he has got no ability to order. Was this a polite suggestion, perhaps? What do you mean by "I personally had to send two battalions who wished to leave their position back to their positions"?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that incident well. This brigade was deployed just outside the village of Negoslavci facing Vukovar. Whenever I was on my way to Vukovar, I would pass that brigade. The commander, as far as I remember, was a colonel, by rank, as far as I remember, but the name escapes me. As a human being and an officer, I did not like the way the commander was treating that unit. He never taught his unit. He was in a cellar somewhere deep in the village of Negoslavci, safely tucked away. Whenever I passed the soldiers, they would always tell me something to that effect. I informed the previous commander of the operations group, since the brigade was subordinated to him, and I informed Colonel Mrksic as well. One day, it so happened, that those people were off, armed, and entered the village of Negoslavci near our command post. They asked to see someone, to speak to someone about that. I think I was the person who happened to be at the command post at the time, and I told the commander that I would be the one to have a word with them. I took off my belt, my rank, my pistol, not sure if I carried a rifle at the time, and I said, "Here I am, bare-handed. Let's see what it is you want to talk about." They talked about some misinformation. They said that three of their own had been killed but not in combat operations. An example, this sabotage group from the paramilitary units was infiltrated into that area, and two snipers climbed up an electricity pylon. The lines were down and this was a flat area, so it was from the top of that pylon at a distance of about 400 to 500 metres that these snipers were shooting at people and they got two of their soldiers. This caused a great deal of panic among these people. I tried to explain why that had happened, that we would be looking into the matter, and later I was reproachful of their commander. And I myself had come under heavy criticism by Colonel Mrksic because I had previously criticised the commander. But I had a word with those people, and those people then went back to their positions. That's what happened, and that's why I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But this was a unit that was subordinated to OG South; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the next day the unit left our area and abandoned those positions, and there is no paper trail of them at any point later on as a unit. This was on the early days of our stay in the area, and I don't remember that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, this was a unit that was subordinated to OG South at that time; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was subordinated in that sense. It was in the area, but there are no references in any of our documents to that unit being a part of OG South, or at least I don't remember. As I say, they immediately left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Forgive me for being cynical, it comes with age, I suppose, but what on earth are you, Major Sljivancanin, doing having a chat with these fellows? Why you? What's it got to do with you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you, haven't I? I happened to be in the building at the time these people came by. They were demonstratively leaving their own area, and they didn't know where to go. They had no one to turn to. I approached the commander to go and have a word with those people. These were our own soldiers after all, they weren't the enemy. We wanted to know where they were going or what they were doing in the area of our command post because that was our command post, after all. All sorts of thoughts were crossing my mind. They might be there to stir some sort of trouble. What did I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Which commander? Are you talking about Mr. Mrksic, or are you talking about someone else?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that the commander was Colonel Bojat, the commander of the operations group when this incident occurred. I am not exactly certain, and don't hold it against me. That was immediately after our arrival in the area. The commander called that colonel, he criticised him, and I know that the unit was then sent back to its position. But I think Bajo Bojat who was the commander at the time, but there might be a certain possibility that I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the reality is it is Bojat who was the commander of OG South that you had dealings with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was at the command post of the Guards Brigade command. What I said is Bojat was in a different house, the OG South command, and Colonel Mrksic was there too. Later on, and I seem to remember that this incident took place when Bojat was still commander, these soldiers came over to the area of our command post. They came over to the house -- to the houses where we were billeted at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But Bojat was OG South, he handed over to Mrksic, or Mrksic took over from Bojat. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I think this incident recorded here occurred while Bojat was still there, but Mrksic said that these people had got as far as the houses where we were staying, and then Bojat called the commander in order to take some measures and the case was resolved. And that's what I remember, and that's why I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I question I asked you is perfectly simple: Bojat -- Mrksic took over from Bojat as the commander of OG South. So what are you dealing -- why are you dealing with something with OG South if you are merely Guards Motorised Brigade? It's got nothing to do with you, has it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain about this incident. I think Bajo Bojat was still commander of the operations group at the time this happened. These military men, they were armed, they came to the area where our command post was, and we were surprised to see them there and we didn't know what they were there for. We took some measures because we didn't know what to do. Those people were just wandering about aimlessly. They didn't know where to go. There has to be some degree of discipline in the area of your command post. Bojat then conducted the interview. They called the commander. They criticised me because I'd raised my voice at this commander, saying wasn't he ashamed that his soldiers were walking around all dissolute like that. I realised that I had been wrong because he held a rank that was higher than mine. But this brought the discussion to an end. What I wish to say by writing this is that certain commanders did not really hold their own units in high esteem. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, look at this paragraph. Just look at it. It's created by you in a way to demonstrate, after conduct of combat operations began, there was a decision issued for the Guards Motorised Brigade commander to take over OG South. That is the core of the paragraph. And then you go on: "Following these decisions, the situation in OG South active zone was much improved. Everything began to function without problems. The greatest difficulty was with the brigade where I personally had to send two battalions who wished to leave their positions back to those positions." What I'm suggesting to you is this paragraph is specifically -- and relates specifically to the transference over to OG South from the Guards Motorised Brigade, how things were improving, and you then describing what the greatest difficulties were. You were dealing with an OG South difficulty. And what I'm asking you is: What are you, Mr. Sljivancanin, doing involving yourself in OG South business if, in actual fact, you were only involved with the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, again, I must say this, it's true what it says here, that it improved. I believe when the commander became the brigade commander, because the brigade was the only one carrying out that task. The other units were not involved in carrying out the mission in Vukovar. But as far as I remember, truly, I believe that this incident involving the Podunavlje Brigade occurred during Bajo Bojat's time as commander of the operations group. It was perhaps of my own impatience I wanted to do something immediately. I was sorry that anything like that was happening in the JNA to begin with, but I thought that the area of our command post, of our Guards Brigade had come under threat, and I thought these persons had no right to dwell in the area. So I talked to the commander, I asked him to go and see what these people were after. So he did. My duty as chief of security was also to supervise or to monitor the area of our brigade, and especially the area of the command post, and I stopped these men well within the area of our command post. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I also am suggesting and will be suggesting to this Court that the functions that you have undertaken in Vukovar have far exceeded your role of a security organ. The phrase "I personally had to send two battalions," there's no discussion, there's no advice. It's quite specific. "I personally had to send," what does that mean, if you didn't have some form of command and control or try and adopt command and control powers?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote in my reports about the situation, about the units that were in the area resting or awaiting a new mission in the area of the Guards Brigade, and I wrote about all the problems. Again, I'm telling you I remember the brigade being just outside the village of Negoslavci facing Vukovar. If you want, I can indicate their position to you on the map. I passed through that area often on my way to Vukovar, and what I wrote here I know that I personally talked to those people when they arrived in the area of the command post of the Guards Brigade, and I tried to turn them around and to impose some discipline. As chief of security, was I perhaps to allow these people to just wander around their own command post area committing breaches of discipline. What was I supposed to do? I accept what you are suggesting. Perhaps my authority was not that great, but what was I to do in this very case? Allowing breaches of discipline in the area of the command post. I said I just go out and see what these people are after and it wasn't my task, but they didn't have their own commander. Who on earth knows where their commanders were. Probably sitting in a house somewhere well away from the front having a drink or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tell me, does the security organ have within its defined task the role of placing soldiers or TOs in various units or under command of various units?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ has no such role. As for the security aspect, they can advise the commander, they can provide their own assessment as to how some people are to be deployed in case the commander can use that sort of information for his intelligence work or anything. But any such advice need not be accepted by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we drop two paragraphs down, please. The paragraph commencing: "In addition to the Guards Motorised Brigade, the Vukovar and Leva Supoderica and a large number of volunteers also participated in the fighting." Have you got that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "The volunteers came in groups individually with no organisation. Our unit had major difficulties in receiving checking and including them and employing them in combat and a large number of volunteers arrived with party insignia which might have had some considerable effects on the order and discipline of the units conducting combat tasks. Through daily and relevant activity, we succeeded in placing all the volunteers under JNA command, i.e., that of OG South." Now, why are you saying "we"? What's it got to do with you if you're a security organ?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this is about is the Guards Brigade command. You see that. I, as a security organ, was part of that command what is included here is the replenishment in manpower levels organ, the logistics organ and the staff as well because the replenishment in manpower level organ was in charge of replenishment and bringing manpower levels up. The equipment organ was in charge of weapons and equipment, and the morale organ was in charge of morale. I'm talking about the command. I was part of command, and I consider myself as security organ to have part of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The next paragraph deals with the government, and I'll try to remember and come back to that in due course. Can we go to the next page, as it is in English, but can you look, please, for the highlight "Guards Motorised Brigade, its combat operations." Have you got that? "OG South command" --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I take it that you, as a security organ, played no part in combat operations, the planning, coordination, et cetera, of those combat operations? Would that be right? Can you just answer the question rather than read the paper for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in planning at all, but I did provide advice and proposals before any decision was taken as to what my views were on how to go about certain missions, especially as concerned my experience on the ground in terms of better ways of dealing with certain missions and avoiding losses or cutting losses. Sometimes my proposals were accepted and sometimes not, depending.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at your participation that you refer to here. "OG South command regularly planned combat operations presumably, not all of which, however, proceeded according to plan. There were certain problems and a drop in combat morale. The first time this happened was on the 6th of October of this year, when I, myself, visited the front combat line to personally encourage the officers and men and give them advice on future activity and the course of the operation." And then you tell us about the death of your driver. Now, what do you mean by "giving them advice on future activity and the course of the operation," if that's outside the ambit of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph you've just read out, that moment, that day, the 6th of October, I'll always remember that day. It was on that day that I lost an honourable and honest man who wasn't even carrying a rifle, just a pistol, no more than a pistol. He was my driver. Didn't fire a single bullet. Or run anybody over, by the way. It was while he was moving near the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion under Major Tesic. He then informed me, Tesic informed me, that he was suffering major losses and that there was heavy fighting underway. He said he had a lot of wounded and that a lot of his men had been killed in the 2nd Company sector along Svetozara Markovica Street. Company commander had requested support, especially in order to evacuate some of the wounded. I was listening to all of that at the time; this was at the outset of fighting. I decided to abandon my vehicle, but my driver did not want to let me go alone. He said: I'll go with you, Major. We got into an APC and this APC was supposed to go and evacuate the wounded. There was a man from Sombor who came with us; he was a reserve sergeant. He said he knew where this place was where these people needed to be evacuated. We got near the house. I don't think I can possibly describe what this was like. There was shooting on all sides. It was difficult to find your way around in that town, and we wanted to take a left turn in order to drive into a yard. We couldn't get through because there was heavy firing meeting us. At one of the gates, there was a heavy military vehicle. We couldn't get through. It had been struck by an anti-tank missile, the front right end of the vehicle. We then got out of the APC. There wasn't much damage. Maybe it was a hand-held rocket that damaged the tank or something like that. But one thing I do know is that Popovic, my driver, got hit by a sniper just after that. I know that the situation in that unit was difficult. I came across the company commander later on, and he told me that the soldiers had been in a state of panic, that they were facing very tough opposition and that I told him the resistance would certainly be on its way very soon, that we shouldn't start running because then there would be more losses, and that we would avoid further casualties by just staying in our positions. So that was the role I had in that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am suggesting to you there are repeated examples of you exercising control, de facto control over and above that which you exercised within the security organ, and this is another example of it. Let us just move down, please, to -- it's three paragraphs below that started, starting "the artillery units played an important part ..."

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Moore, that is your conclusion, but find me a document which says that I exercised any control of that kind. To assist a wounded soldier and to help soldiers not to be taken by panic is the task of any officer, whether he be a security officer or holds whatever post, and that was the task that I was discharging at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just deal with this very quickly. I seem to remember it relates to an incident on the 20th, 21st of October where there was defective artillery fire. Do you see the sentence starting: "The artillery units played an important part in the liberation of Vukovar, but there were incidents of friendly fire. Following what I saw at the front line, I informed the commander, held a meeting. After that, there were no targeting errors at all." Is this the incident of the 20th, 21st of October that we have heard evidence about, and I believe there is a reference to it in the Guards war diary? Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to that event. I have said everything that I know about that event. I thought that this was such a meeting. The colonel then had brought the division commanders to the observation post, but they came there primarily with a fact of dissuading me, to convince me that I was not right, that I was wrong, but they actually came to -- found out that I was right, and that is why I wrote that this meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And isn't it also right to say that on one occasion, in relation to artillery fire, you had, I believe, computer control of the guns, of the howitzers, that an individual refused to give coordinates to the gunners because of the concern that he had for inaccurate fire; isn't that right? He actually refused to give the coordinates because the firing was so bad.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question, but let me tell you this: I am really not an artillery officer, and I know what target redistribution and correction of fire is but I cannot operate artillery pieces and never have. But I have observed many an exercise and I went to different tactical meetings where artillery units were also presented to us, and I know what they are supposed to do, but I never controlled any computer fire of howitzers, nor am I professionally capable or trained for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you have never heard of an officer refusing to give the coordinates to facilitate artillery fire because the results had been so bad? You never heard of that, the firing had been so inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a case of inaccurate fire and I have said that before. When I was in the area of the 1st Platoon for anti-terrorist activity and I collected information from other people who informed me as I was touring the different areas, namely they told me that there was imprecise shooting by the artillery units in the 1st Military District, which is why I did what I did, let me not repeat that. But this what you are now saying, that is something that I can not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us finish with this document by going to the conclusion. Can we look at conclusion number 5, conclusion number 6. These are your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "The placing of all groups, individuals and units under OG South command had a very positive effect." Yes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found that task. I believe that it was positive for one command to be in that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then number 6: "The work of the Guards Motorised Brigade security organ, officers in processing prisoners and undertaking all the security measures ordered and in providing security in the zone of active combat was particularly well-organised and professional." Is that you? Is that you saying that in actual fact it was your unit -- was particularly well-organised and professional?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I always thought and I still do that the security organs of the Guards Motorised Brigade performed their work in a professional way and controlled their zone professionally and discharged their tasks properly and there were no -- I didn't notice that anything was being done in an unorganised or irregular fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And processing prisoners? This is the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Processing prisoners, I primarily meant the processing of prisoners during the very operation of the deblocking of the barracks and the disarming of paramilitaries. Because from the 18th, there were no more processings of prisoners because the orders were that they were all to be sent to Sremska Mitrovica. We no longer, from that date, dealt with them because they would be -- they were all sent to Mitrovica then. Before that, we were supposed to send prisoners to Sid, as soon as possible, but before sending them we had to conduct an interview with them in order to ascertain what units, what forces were ahead of our own units, if those people were able to impart that information to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sir, what are you saying, that processing prisoners, the term "processing prisoners," really only relates up to the 18th of November? What you describe then -- or what title do you ascribe then to the prisoners taken after the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had specific orders then not to detain and not to conduct any interviews with the people, but to send them to the collection centre in Sremska Mitrovica where the proper authorities would deal with them. And the combat operations stopped so that we no longer needed to collect information on the disposition of paramilitary units ahead of our own units, and those were the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I finish today with the following question: When was it that you say you actually heard firstly rumours that there had been atrocities committed in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of that, for the first time, seriously, in 1995. And as I have said, I do not deny that there have been rumours in some sections of the media which I called "tabloids" and there was a lot of misinformation planted in such media. They tried to also mount a smear campaign against me personally, whereas others commended me. So I didn't want to devote any time to that and I mostly did not read any of that. But it was in 1995 that I learned most of the pertinent information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So are you saying, then, that no former officer or officer or any member of any administration ever contacted you, Mr. Sljivancanin, the chief of the security organ of the Guards Motorised Brigade, about the atrocities at Ovcara? Is that what you're actually saying?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time it was I, myself, that asked, in 1995. Having heard about it, I asked to see the chief of the General Staff for the truth to be ascertained for the sake of the truth and dignity and to see what measures needed to be taken. The chief of the General Staff received me. I asked to be also received by the chief of the security administration who said that he would summon me when needed via his secretary, and he called me for a talk for the first time in February 1998, if I'm not wrong. And then again I also went to see the military prosecutor in the military court, General Obrencevic, if I remembered his name correctly. Both the chief of the General Staff and the military prosecutor promised saying that they knew that this certainly did not refer to me, but they promised that they will take all the necessary measures for action to be taken in that regard and that we would know what course to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
