utterances.text: General Kadijevic was a man you knew, whom you respected, and you knew his brothers and family, I think; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic was a man -- is a man whom I still hold in the highest of esteems, and I knew his wife Ozrenka very well. I knew his brothers, the wives of his brothers, and I think that this is a decent, decent family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, would you be kind enough to turn up tab 18 and tab 19 -- sorry, 17 and 18. In actual fact, it is just tab 18 because of the translation difficulties which I mentioned. Just tab 18. I'd like you to look at the date on the right-hand corner. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have here is an act called the secretariat --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, sorry. The interpreter is lost. Can the witness please repeat this more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to tab 18, and you will find, I hope -- so tab 18, you'll find an English version and you will find beneath it the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have it. I thought you had said 17. Well, it says "General Veljko Kadijevic" in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I ask the question, please. Here is a letter dated the 9th of December, 1991, going to the head of the armed forces at that time, General Kadijevic. That's the same gentleman you speak so highly about. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is addressed to General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. The first paragraph deals with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has another objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have an objection. I just can see that Mr. Sljivancanin has the English version in front of him, and knowing that his English is not that good, I just wanted to ask him to turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got the B/C/S version? It seems to me you have.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back. So we've got -- going to General Kadijevic. It's the British Medical Association out of Tavistock Square. I'd like to go to the second paragraph. "I am writing to you to appeal for information about the fate of some 500 patients and medical staff who were said to have been evacuated by the JNA from the Vukovar Hospital last month. When the army entered Vukovar, it was estimated that an approximate total of 440 patients were being treated in the hospital by 320 staff. Only 120 patients and 72 health professionals have since been returned to the Croatian authorities. We understand that the acting head of the hospital, Dr. Vesna Bosanac, and her assistant, Dr. Njavro, have been taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica together with a wounded journalist, Mr. Glavasevic, and his Serbian colleague, Mr. Polovina. The remaining patients and staff apparently appear to be missing. Evidence put forward by Amnesty International indicates that all sides of the conflict have committed atrocities, including the extrajudicial execution or arbitrary or deliberate killing of unarmed civilians and wounded or surrendering combatants. We are seeking the help of the authorities in Belgrade to trace the whereabouts of those who worked or were treated in the Vukovar Hospital and would urgently request your assistance." Now, this is a letter from the BMA, it's going to Kadijevic, it's asking specifically about the evacuation that you had responsibility for. Are you saying that Kadijevic never ever spoke to you about the general problems that may have arisen at the Vukovar evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, you said that I was responsible for an evacuation. I was not in charge of any evacuation, including that of the Vukovar Hospital. I only was in charge of security tasks and that is what I did. So General Kadijevic never invited me in connection with these issues, nor did I ever have any talk with him on that subject. As regards this letter which you have just read, I received that letter in the batch of documents that were given to me at the Detention Unit in The Hague, and now I see that, you just having read out for me, I didn't know about it before nor did I ever discuss this subject with General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Time, Mr. Moore, time has slipped by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Too slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Too slowly, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answers are very long. I don't wish to be discourteous to Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answers undoubtedly at times are long, as are some questions, as are the scope of what you're trying to deal with it. We resume tomorrow at 2.15 in, I believe, Courtroom I. I see everyone wants a star performance. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already talked with Mr. Moore. This is just a technical question. Will he be finishing possibly tomorrow because of the next witness. He has announced that he will be questioning this witness all day tomorrow. I presume he has not changed his plan and pace. So shall we plan to bring our witness for the next day, I mean for tomorrow or not? This is just what I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, can you help?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I did indicate to my learned friend that I felt that I would finish on the Wednesday. It may well be that Your Honour takes a view the scope is too broad, but the reality is, I have other topics to go through. I wanted to get through these documents and then move on to, shall I say the more factual evidence, and I will move as quickly as I possibly can. The only way I can move on quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean Thursday, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope to finish my cross-examination tomorrow, but I am worried now that it may slip into Thursday, and I don't want that to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, your witness Thursday, not tomorrow, even if we lose a bit of time if Mr. Moore overcomes his problems. Now, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was waiting for the moment for a segment to be finished so as to state my view on the submission of documents. The introduction of documents, the admission of documents, so I have a position to make clear. When would it be convenient for Your Honours? Would it be the time now or perhaps in the morning, tomorrow? I just wanted to announce this in time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter apologises. She had already taken her headphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This would only take a very short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, we are already 10 minutes over time and delaying the next trial's commencement by 10 minutes as a result. We do not propose to interrupt the evidence of Mr. Sljivancanin to deal with the question of the admission of documents. But as soon as his evidence is finished, we would allow no more than 10 minutes for all submissions about the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.
